source: The key proteins mediating oxygen sensing in these cells involve two classes of proteins: (1) upstream oxygen sensors, namely the prolyl hydroxylases EglN1–3, responsible for the hydroxylation of various substrates, such as hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF), FOXO3a, ADSL, SFMBT1, and TBK1 (Hu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Semenza, 2012; Zheng et al., 2014; Zurlo et al., 2019); (2) the downstream VHL E3 ligase complex.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Semenza, 2012; Zheng et al., 2014; Zurlo et al., 2019

claim: EglN family members (EglN1, primarily in vivo) hydroxylate HIF1α on proline 402 and 564 positions.
source: For example, EglN family members (EglN1, primarily in vivo) hydroxylate HIF1α on proline 402 and 564 positions, which lead to pVHL binding and HIF1α ubiquitination and degradation (Appelhoff et al., 2004; Ivan et al., 2001; Jaakkola et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Appelhoff et al., 2004; Ivan et al., 2001; Jaakkola et al., 2001

claim: Hydroxylation of HIF1α on proline 402 and 564 positions leads to pVHL binding and HIF1α ubiquitination and degradation.
source: For example, EglN family members (EglN1, primarily in vivo) hydroxylate HIF1α on proline 402 and 564 positions, which lead to pVHL binding and HIF1α ubiquitination and degradation (Appelhoff et al., 2004; Ivan et al., 2001; Jaakkola et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Appelhoff et al., 2004; Ivan et al., 2001; Jaakkola et al., 2001

source: HIF1α has been well established to be an important oncogene in multiple cancers, including breast cancer (Briggs et al., 2016; Semenza, 2010).

claim: Tumor hypoxia or pVHL loss will lead to the accumulation of HIF1α.
source: Tumor hypoxia or pVHL loss will lead to the accumulation of HIF1α.
evidence: Stated as established scientific knowledge

claim: HIF1α dimerizes with a constitutively expressed HIF1β subunit (also called ARNT) in the nucleus.
source: As a result of the accumulation and translocation of HIFα factors into the nucleus, HIF1α dimerizes with a constitutively expressed HIF1β subunit (also called ARNT) and transactivates genes that have hypoxia response elements (HREs, sequence: NCGTG) in promoters or enhancer regions.
evidence: Stated as established scientific knowledge

claim: HIF1α transactivates genes that have hypoxia response elements (HREs, sequence: NCGTG) in promoters or enhancer regions.

claim: HIF1-transactivated genes include those involved in angiogenesis (e.g., VEGF), glycolysis and glucose transport (e.g., SLC2A1), and erythropoiesis (e.g., EPO).
source: HIF1-transactivated genes include those involved in angiogenesis (e.g., VEGF), glycolysis and glucose transport (e.g., SLC2A1), and erythropoiesis (e.g., EPO) (Semenza, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Semenza, 2012

claim: ZHX2 is amplified in various cancers, including ovarian cancer (~40%) and breast cancer (~15%).
source: Analysis of copy number across different cancer types from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) showed that ZHX2 is amplified in various cancers, including ovarian cancer (~40%) and breast cancer (~15%) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by data analysis from TCGA shown in Figure 1A

claim: ZHX2 and MYC share coamplification in most cancer types observed.
source: Importantly, ZHX2 and MYC share coamplification in most cancer types observed (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B

claim: ZHX2 is not amplified in ccRCC.
source: Interestingly, ZHX2 is not amplified in ccRCC (referred as KIRC in Figure 1A,B), where it is regulated mainly post-transcriptionally by pVHL loss in this cancer (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A,B and citation to Zhang et al., 2018

claim: ZHX2 is regulated mainly post-transcriptionally by pVHL loss in ccRCC.
source: Interestingly, ZHX2 is not amplified in ccRCC (referred as KIRC in Figure 1A,B), where it is regulated mainly post-transcriptionally by pVHL loss in this cancer (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018

claim: TNBC had the highest ZHX2 amplification rate in all breast cancer subtypes.
source: Detailed analyses of several breast cancer patient datasets also revealed that TNBC had the highest ZHX2 amplification rate in all breast cancer subtypes (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1a

claim: There is a significant correlation between ZHX2 copy number and gene expression in breast cancer.
source: Next, we performed correlation studies to examine the copy number gain of ZHX2 and its expression in TCGA (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012) and METABRIC datasets (Curtis et al., 2012 Figure 1D). We found a significant correlation between copy number and gene expression (Figure 1D), suggesting that ZHX2 amplification may be at least partially responsible for its overexpression in breast cancer.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1D using TCGA and METABRIC datasets

claim: ZHX2 amplification may be at least partially responsible for its overexpression in breast cancer.
source: We found a significant correlation between copy number and gene expression (Figure 1D), suggesting that ZHX2 amplification may be at least partially responsible for its overexpression in breast cancer.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between copy number and expression shown in Figure 1D

claim: ZHX2 overexpression (Affymetrix probe 236169_at) correlates with worse survival in TNBC but not in other breast cancer subtypes.
source: We further explored the effect of ZHX2 expression on breast cancer patient survival. ZHX2 overexpression (Affymetrix probe 236169_at) correlates with worse survival in TNBC but not in other breast cancer subtypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: All breast cancer cell lines displayed relatively higher ZHX2 protein levels compared to HMLE or MCF-10A.
source: We obtained a panel of breast cancer cell lines as well as two immortalized normal breast epithelial cell lines, HMLE and MCF-10A. Interestingly, all breast cancer cell lines displayed relatively higher ZHX2 protein levels compared to HMLE or MCF-10A (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1E

claim: ZHX2 was upregulated in the majority of TNBC patient tumors compared to normal (8 out of 10).
source: We detected ZHX2 protein level in 10 pairs of TNBC patient tumors and their respective normal control (Supplementary file 1b). Consistently, ZHX2 was upregulated in the majority of tumors compared to normal (8 out of 10) (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by western blot data from patient samples shown in Figure 1F

claim: ZHX2 staining was increased in TNBC tumors, especially in the nuclear staining by quantification.
source: To strengthen the clinical significance of ZHX2, we also performed immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining in 20 pairs of normal/tumor TNBC patient parafilm tissue slides and found an overall increased ZHX2 staining in the TNBC tumors, especially in the nuclear staining by quantification (Figure 1G, H), suggesting overall and the nuclear located ZHX2 is upregulated in tumors from TNBC patients.
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1G, H

claim: Overall and the nuclear located ZHX2 is upregulated in tumors from TNBC patients.
source: To strengthen the clinical significance of ZHX2, we also performed immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining in 20 pairs of normal/tumor TNBC patient parafilm tissue slides and found an overall increased ZHX2 staining in the TNBC tumors, especially in the nuclear staining by quantification (Figure 1G, H), suggesting overall and the nuclear located ZHX2 is upregulated in tumors from TNBC patients.
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1G, H

claim: All TNBC cell lines displayed relatively lower pVHL protein levels corresponding with higher ZHX2 protein level when compared to normal breast cells.
source: To this purpose, we first examined the relationship between the expression of ZHX2 and pVHL in several TNBC cell lines (MDA-MB-231, MDA-MB-436, MDA-MB-468, HCC3153, and HCC70) as well as two normal breast epithelial cell lines, HMLE and MCF-10A. Interestingly, all TNBC cell lines displayed relatively lower pVHL protein levels corresponding with higher ZHX2 protein level when compared to normal breast cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: ZHX2 interacts with pVHL in two representative TNBC cell lines.
source: Our co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) experiments showed that ZHX2 interacts with pVHL in two representative TNBC cell lines (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 1I

claim: pVHL overexpression leads to decreased ZHX2 protein levels in MDA-MB-231 and 468 cells.
source: First, we overexpressed HA-VHL in two different TNBC cell lines (MDA-MB-231 and 468) and found that pVHL overexpression leads to decreased ZHX2 protein levels (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1J

claim: pVHL depletion led to upregulation of ZHX2 protein in MDA-MB-231 and 468 cells.
source: Conversely, we also deleted VHL expression by three independent sgRNAs (#1, 2, and 8) in these two cell lines and found that pVHL depletion led to upregulation of ZHX2 protein (Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1K and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: ZHX2 regulation by pVHL potentially depends on ZHX2 prolyl hydroxylation.
source: Our previous research showed that ZHX2 regulation by pVHL potentially depends on ZHX2 prolyl hydroxylation (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018

claim: ZHX2 was upregulated by hypoxia, DMOG, or MG132 treatment in MDA-MB-231 and 468 cells.
source: We treated these two cell lines with hypoxia, the pan-prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor DMOG, or the proteasomal inhibitor MG132 and found that ZHX2 was upregulated by these treatments (Figure 1L, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), further strengthening the conclusion that ZHX2 is regulated by pVHL for protein stability through potential prolyl hydroxylation in breast cancer.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1L and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E

claim: ZHX2 is regulated by pVHL for protein stability through potential prolyl hydroxylation in breast cancer.
source: We treated these two cell lines with hypoxia, the pan-prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor DMOG, or the proteasomal inhibitor MG132 and found that ZHX2 was upregulated by these treatments (Figure 1L, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), further strengthening the conclusion that ZHX2 is regulated by pVHL for protein stability through potential prolyl hydroxylation in breast cancer.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing ZHX2 upregulation by hypoxia, DMOG, and MG132

claim: ZHX2 was upregulated in most of tumor tissues compared to normal, coinciding with decreased pVHL protein levels in respective tumor tissues.
source: We further analyzed ZHX2 and pVHL protein levels in 10 pairs of TNBC tumors and paired normal tissue (Supplementary file 1b). In accordance with the cell line data, we found that ZHX2 was upregulated in most of tumor tissues compared to normal, coinciding with decreased pVHL protein levels in respective tumor tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by western blot data from patient samples shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F

claim: There is an overall negative correlation between pVHL and ZHX2 in TNBC samples.
source: We performed IHC staining to the TMA with ZHX2 and pVHL antibody and scored the IHC staining intensities (Detre et al., 1995) of each specimen for these two proteins, respectively. We found an overall negative correlation between pVHL and ZHX2 in these TNBC samples which were divided into different staining grades based on the staining intensity (Figure 1M, N and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1M, N and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G

claim: ZHX2 is regulated by pVHL and play an important role in TNBC.
source: In conclusion, our data suggest that ZHX2 is regulated by pVHL and play an important role in TNBC.
evidence: Inferred from the collective experimental results showing ZHX2-pVHL interaction and regulation

claim: ZHX2 depletion led to decreased cell proliferation in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells.
source: Next, we found that ZHX2 depletion led to decreased cell proliferation, 2D colony formation as well as 3D soft agar growth in both cell lines (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 2C

claim: ZHX2 depletion led to decreased 2D colony formation in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells.
source: Next, we found that ZHX2 depletion led to decreased cell proliferation, 2D colony formation as well as 3D soft agar growth in both cell lines (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: Supported by 2D colony formation assay data shown in Figure 2D

claim: ZHX2 depletion led to decreased 3D soft agar growth in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells.
source: Next, we found that ZHX2 depletion led to decreased cell proliferation, 2D colony formation as well as 3D soft agar growth in both cell lines (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: Supported by 3D soft agar assay data shown in Figure 2E, F

claim: ZHX2 depletion led to decreased cell invasion in TNBC cell lines.
source: Consistent with the results above, ZHX2 depletion led to decreased cell invasion in these TNBC cell lines (Figure 2G, H).
evidence: Supported by invasion assay data shown in Figure 2G, H

claim: ZHX2 shRNA-induced phenotypes in TNBC cells could be completely rescued by shRNA-resistant ZHX2 in two TNBC cell lines.
source: We also showed that ZHX2 shRNA-induced phenotypes in TNBC cells could be completely rescued by shRNA-resistant ZHX2 in two TNBC cell lines (Figure 2I–N and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–G), suggesting that these phenotypes were due to on-target depletion of ZHX2 by shRNAs.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2I–N and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–G

claim: The phenotypes observed with ZHX2 shRNA were due to on-target depletion of ZHX2 by shRNAs.
source: We also showed that ZHX2 shRNA-induced phenotypes in TNBC cells could be completely rescued by shRNA-resistant ZHX2 in two TNBC cell lines (Figure 2I–N and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–G), suggesting that these phenotypes were due to on-target depletion of ZHX2 by shRNAs.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue experiments showing restoration of phenotype with shRNA-resistant ZHX2

claim: ZHX2 depletion significantly decreased tumor growth over time in MDA-MB-231 orthotopic xenografts.
source: We found that ZHX2 depletion significantly decreased tumor growth overtime (Figure 3B), as well as reduced tumor burden retrieved from tumor-bearing mice compared to control mice upon necropsy (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: Supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 3B

claim: ZHX2 depletion reduced tumor burden retrieved from tumor-bearing mice compared to control mice upon necropsy.
source: We found that ZHX2 depletion significantly decreased tumor growth overtime (Figure 3B), as well as reduced tumor burden retrieved from tumor-bearing mice compared to control mice upon necropsy (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: Supported by tumor weight and image data shown in Figure 3C, D

claim: ZHX2 depletion led to significantly decreased lung metastasis in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Given the high in vivo lung metastatic feature of MDA-MB-231 (Jin et al., 2020), we measured spontaneous lung metastasis ex vivo upon necropsy and found that ZHX2 depletion led to significantly decreased lung metastasis in MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 3F, G).
evidence: Supported by lung metastasis data shown in Figure 3F, G

claim: ZHX2 depletion mainly affected proliferation for the tumor cells reflected by marked decrease of Ki-67 in ZHX2 depleted tumor, rather than angiogenesis or apoptosis.
source: IHC assays showed that ZHX2 depletion mainly affected proliferation for the tumor cells reflected by marked decrease of Ki-67 in ZHX2 depleted tumor, rather than angiogenesis or apoptosis (Figure 3L and M).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3L and M

claim: Knockdown ZHX2 did not affect protein level of c-Myc.
source: Although ZHX2 and c-Myc displayed similar amplification and expression manner in breast cancer (Figure 1A, B, E). Our data showed that knockdown ZHX2 did not affect protein level of c-Myc (Figure 3A, H), suggesting the oncogenic function of ZHX2 is independent of c-Myc in TNBC cells.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A, H

claim: The oncogenic function of ZHX2 is independent of c-Myc in TNBC cells.
source: Although ZHX2 and c-Myc displayed similar amplification and expression manner in breast cancer (Figure 1A, B, E). Our data showed that knockdown ZHX2 did not affect protein level of c-Myc (Figure 3A, H), suggesting the oncogenic function of ZHX2 is independent of c-Myc in TNBC cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ZHX2 knockdown does not affect c-Myc levels

claim: ZHX2 is important for TNBC cell proliferation and tumorigenesis in vivo.
source: Taken together, our data strongly indicate that ZHX2 is important for TNBC cell proliferation and tumorigenesis in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the collective in vivo experimental results

claim: ZHX2 did not consistently and robustly bind with p65 in TNBC cells.
source: We first examined the interaction of ZHX2 and p65 in breast cancer by endogenous IP with ZHX2 or p65 antibody in two TNBC cells (MDA-MB-231 and 468) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B), we did not find consistent and robust binding between ZHX2 and p65 as we observed in ccRCC.
evidence: Supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: Knockdown of ZHX2 did not change the gross p65 protein level.
source: In addition, knockdown of ZHX2 also did not change the gross p65 protein level (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), or the subcellular protein level of p65 either in cytosol or nucleus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: Knockdown of ZHX2 did not change the subcellular protein level of p65 either in cytosol or nucleus.
source: In addition, knockdown of ZHX2 also did not change the gross p65 protein level (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), or the subcellular protein level of p65 either in cytosol or nucleus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E

claim: ZHX2 may not affect NF-κB signaling in TNBC.
source: Altogether, these data suggest ZHX2 may not affect NF-κB signaling in TNBC.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of interaction between ZHX2 and p65 and lack of effect on p65 levels

claim: Two individual ZHX2 shRNAs concordantly altered gene expression patterns in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: In order to determine the molecular mechanism by which ZHX2 contributes to TNBC, we performed RNA-seq analyses in MDA-MB-231 cells with two independent ZHX2 shRNAs (sh43 and sh45) and found that two individual shRNAs concordantly altered gene expression patterns (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A, B

claim: Genes differentially expressed following ZHX2 depletion were enriched for members of the hypoxia pathway.
source: Pathway enrichment as well as gene set enrichment analyses (GSEAs) revealed that genes differentially expressed following ZHX2 depletion were enriched for members of the hypoxia pathway (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment and GSEA data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: The NF-κB pathway was not enriched through RNA-seq analysis following ZHX2 depletion.
source: Consistent with the lack of regulation of NF-κB components by ZHX2 by IP and western blots, we did not find the NF-κB pathway being enriched through our RNA-seq analysis pathway (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A

claim: There were 7690 genes differentially expressed following ZHX2 silencing by shRNA.
source: Overall, there were 7690 genes differentially expressed following ZHX2 silencing by shRNA, and 1849 (24%) of these genes overlapped with genes differentially expressed in a previously published HIF1A and HIF2A double knockout (HIF DKO) model (Figure 4D; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4D

claim: 1849 (24%) of genes differentially expressed following ZHX2 silencing overlapped with genes differentially expressed in a HIF1A and HIF2A double knockout (HIF DKO) model.
source: Overall, there were 7690 genes differentially expressed following ZHX2 silencing by shRNA, and 1849 (24%) of these genes overlapped with genes differentially expressed in a previously published HIF1A and HIF2A double knockout (HIF DKO) model (Figure 4D; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4D and citation to Chen et al., 2018

claim: 678 genes (17%) of ZHX2 positively regulated genes overlapped with downregulated genes in the HIF DKO RNA-seq, representing a significant association (adj. p = 1.07 × 10−69).
source: Of these, 678 genes (17%) overlapped with downregulated genes in the HIF DKO RNA-seq (Figure 4E), representing a significant association (adj. p = 1.07 × 10−69).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4E

claim: The overlap between ZHX2 positively regulated genes and HIF DKO downregulated genes strengthens the potential functional link between HIF and ZHX2.
source: Of these, 678 genes (17%) overlapped with downregulated genes in the HIF DKO RNA-seq (Figure 4E), representing a significant association (adj. p = 1.07 × 10−69). These data strengthen the potential functional link between HIF and ZHX2.
evidence: Inferred from the significant overlap between ZHX2 and HIF regulated genes

claim: Hypoxia treatment increased the expression of HIF target genes, and this effect was ameliorated by ZHX2 depletion.
source: Based on our ZHX2 RNA-seq and GSEA results (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C), we chose a few representative HIF target genes and examined their expression levels by qRT-PCR in MDA-MB-231 cells infected with control or ZHX2 shRNA under either normoxia or hypoxia. As expected, hypoxia treatment increased the expression of HIF target genes, and this effect was ameliorated by ZHX2 depletion (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that ZHX2 affects HIF activity and regulates HIF target gene expression in TNBC.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D

claim: ZHX2 affects HIF activity and regulates HIF target gene expression in TNBC.
source: As expected, hypoxia treatment increased the expression of HIF target genes, and this effect was ameliorated by ZHX2 depletion (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that ZHX2 affects HIF activity and regulates HIF target gene expression in TNBC.
evidence: Inferred from the qRT-PCR results showing ZHX2 depletion ameliorates hypoxia-induced HIF target gene expression

claim: ZHX2 depletion led to decreased HIF reporter activity.
source: Consistently, HIF reporter assay found that ZHX2 depletion led to decreased HIF reporter activity while ZHX2 re-expression could rescue this phenomenon either under normoxia or hypoxia (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by HIF reporter assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E

claim: ZHX2 re-expression could rescue the decreased HIF reporter activity caused by ZHX2 depletion either under normoxia or hypoxia.
source: Consistently, HIF reporter assay found that ZHX2 depletion led to decreased HIF reporter activity while ZHX2 re-expression could rescue this phenomenon either under normoxia or hypoxia (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by HIF reporter assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E

claim: ZHX2 activated HIF reporter activity in a dose-dependent manner.
source: In addition, ZHX2 activated HIF reporter activity in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Supported by HIF reporter assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2F

claim: ZHX2 bound with HIF1α and HIF1β exogenously as well as endogenously.
source: Next, to gain further insight on how ZHX2 affect the HIF signaling. Consider a well characterization on HIF1 function in TNBC tumorigenesis by previous studies (Bos et al., 2001; Briggs et al., 2016). We first performed Co-IP experiments and showed that ZHX2 bound with HIF1α and HIF1β exogenously as well as endogenously (Figure 4F–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: Supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 4F–H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2G

claim: ZHX2 knockdown led to decreased HIF1α protein levels in two TNBC cell lines under hypoxia condition.
source: In addition, ZHX2 knockdown led to decreased HIF1α protein levels in two TNBC cell lines under hypoxia condition (Figure 4I, J).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4I, J

claim: ZHX2 overexpression led to increased HIF1α protein levels under normoxia.
source: Conversely, ZHX2 overexpression led to increased HIF1α protein levels under normoxia (Figure 4K).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4K

claim: ZHX2 loss-of-function or gain-of-function manipulations did not grossly change HIF2α protein level.
source: However, these ZHX2 loss-of-function or gain-of-function manipulations did not grossly change HIF2α protein level (Figure 4J, K).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4J, K

source: Co-IP experiments showed that ZHX2 could not bind with HIF2α (Figure 4L).
evidence: Supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 4L

claim: ZHX2 regulates the hypoxia signaling mainly through HIF1α.
source: These results suggest that ZHX2 regulates the hypoxia signaling mainly through HIF1α.
evidence: Inferred from the observations that ZHX2 binds and regulates HIF1α but not HIF2α

claim: ZHX2 overexpression did not increase HIF1A mRNA level.
source: Interestingly, qRT-PCR showed that ZHX2 overexpression did not increase HIF1A mRNA level (Figure 4M), suggesting a mechanism of post-transcriptional regulation on HIF1α.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4M

claim: ZHX2 regulates HIF1α through a mechanism of post-transcriptional regulation.
source: Interestingly, qRT-PCR showed that ZHX2 overexpression did not increase HIF1A mRNA level (Figure 4M), suggesting a mechanism of post-transcriptional regulation on HIF1α.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ZHX2 overexpression increases HIF1α protein but not mRNA

claim: MG132 treatment could fully rescue the HIF1α protein level in ZHX2 knockdown cells under hypoxia.
source: We then treated the ZHX2 knockdown cells with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 under hypoxia, which could fully rescue the HIF1α protein level in the knockdown cells (Figure 4N).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4N

claim: Overexpression of ZHX2 could protect HIF1α from ubiquitination and subsequent degradation.
source: Our ubiquitination assay also showed that overexpression of ZHX2 could protect HIF1α from ubiquitination and subsequent degradation (Figure 4O).
evidence: Supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4O

claim: ZHX2 controls HIF1α protein stability by preventing proteasome-mediated degradation.

evidence: Inferred from the MG132 rescue and ubiquitination assay results

claim: HIF1α knockdown did not affect ZHX2 protein levels.

evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2H

claim: 94% of ZHX2 binding sites overlap with H3K27ac.
source: We identified 957 binding sites across the genome, of which 94% of them overlap with H3K27ac and 96% of them overlap with H3K4me3 (Figure 5A), indicating these overlapping peaks bound preferentially to active promoters for gene expression (Shlyueva et al., 2014).

claim: 96% of ZHX2 binding sites overlap with H3K4me3.

evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A

claim: ZHX2 binding sites overlapping with H3K27ac and H3K4me3 bound preferentially to active promoters for gene expression.

evidence: Supported by citation to Shlyueva et al., 2014 and ChIP-seq data

claim: ZHX2 positively regulated gene promoters (n = 258) demonstrated robust enrichment for HIF1α, H3K4me3, and H3K27ac.
source: We again focused on the ZHX2 positively regulated genes (downregulated following ZHX2 silencing by shRNA) that exhibited ZHX2 binding in the promoter (transcription start site ±5 kb). These promoters (n = 258) demonstrated robust enrichment for HIF1α (Chen et al., 2018), as well as H3K4me3 and H3K27ac (Rhie et al., 2014; Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A and citations to Chen et al., 2018; Rhie et al., 2014

claim: Seven candidate genes (PTGES3L, KDM3A, WSB1, AP2B1, OXSR1, RUNDC1, and COX20) were identified as bound and positively regulated by both ZHX2 and HIF1α.
source: We then filtered these genes further, focusing on only those bound and positively regulated by HIF1α and identified seven interesting candidate genes for follow-up functional validation (PTGES3L, KDM3A, WSB1, AP2B1, OXSR1, RUNDC1, and COX20).
evidence: Identified through integrated ChIP-seq and RNA-seq analysis

claim: ZHX2 depletion by shRNAs led to decreased mRNA expression for PTGES3L, KDM3A, WSB1, AP2B1, OXSR1, RUNDC1, and COX20.
source: We performed qRT-PCR analysis and found that ZHX2 depletion by shRNAs indeed led to decreased mRNA expression for all of these target genes (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B

claim: ZHX2 overexpression led to increased expression of PTGES3L, KDM3A, WSB1, AP2B1, OXSR1, RUNDC1, and COX20.
source: Conversely, we also overexpressed ZHX2 in TNBC cells and found that ZHX2 overexpression led to increased expression of these target genes (Figure 5C), arguing that ZHX2 promotes HIF signaling by at least directly activating these targets in TNBC.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C

claim: ZHX2 promotes HIF signaling by at least directly activating PTGES3L, KDM3A, WSB1, AP2B1, OXSR1, RUNDC1, and COX20 in TNBC.
source: Conversely, we also overexpressed ZHX2 in TNBC cells and found that ZHX2 overexpression led to increased expression of these target genes (Figure 5C), arguing that ZHX2 promotes HIF signaling by at least directly activating these targets in TNBC.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ZHX2 binds to and regulates expression of these genes

claim: HIF depletion led to decreased expression of PTGES3L, KDM3A, WSB1, AP2B1, OXSR1, RUNDC1, and COX20 under hypoxic conditions.
source: To further strengthen whether these are HIF downstream target genes, we also obtained HIF DKO cells and found that HIF depletion led to decreased expression of these target genes under hypoxic conditions (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D

claim: ZHX2 binds with HIF and affects HIF activity in TNBC.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that ZHX2 binds with HIF and affects HIF activity in TNBC.
evidence: Inferred from the collective experimental results showing ZHX2-HIF interaction and co-regulation of target genes

claim: At least four genes (AP2B1, COX20, KDM3A, and PTGES3L) could partially rescue the growth defect caused by ZHX2 depletion.
source: We then performed 2D colony formation assays and found that at least four genes (AP2B1, COX20, KDM3A, and PTGES3L) could partially rescue the growth by ZHX2 depletion (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by 2D colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5F

claim: The downstream targets AP2B1, COX20, KDM3A, and PTGES3L contribute to the oncogenic role of ZHX2 in an accumulative fashion.

evidence: Inferred from the partial rescue observed with individual target gene overexpression

claim: Arg491 in HD2, Arg581 in HD3, and Arg674 in HD4 are the most contacted residues in DNA binding.
source: We found that Lys485/Arg491 in HD2, Arg581 in HD3, and Arg674 in HD4 are the most contacted residues in DNA binding, where Arg674 receives the highest contact among all the HD proteins.
evidence: Supported by structural modeling and contact analysis

claim: Arg674 receives the highest contact among all the HD proteins.
source: We found that Lys485/Arg491 in HD2, Arg581 in HD3, and Arg674 in HD4 are the most contacted residues in DNA binding, where Arg674 receives the highest contact among all the HD proteins.
evidence: Supported by structural modeling and contact analysis

claim: Arg491 in HD2, Arg581 in HD3, and Arg674 in HD4 have the highest affinity with DNA in terms of MM/PBSA-derived contact potential energies.
source: Our molecular dynamics (MD) simulations further revealed that Arg491 in HD2, Arg581 in HD3, and Arg674 in HD4 indeed have the highest affinity with DNA, in terms of molecular mechanics Poisson–Boltzmann surface area (MM/PBSA)-derived contact potential energies (see Supplementary file 1d,e Videos 1–3), among other residues in the same proteins.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data

claim: Residues Asp489 (D489), Arg491 (R491), Glu579 (E579), Arg581 (R581), Lys582 (K582), Arg674 (R674), Glu678 (E678), and Arg680 (R680) are important for ZHX2 binding to DNA.
source: Among the top 4 DNA-contacting residues in each of the HD proteins, we consider those with relatively high sequence conservation being important for ZHX2 binding to DNA, which may affect the phenotype of TNBC. These residues are Asp489 (D489), Arg491 (R491), Glu579 (E579), Arg581 (R581), Lys582 (K582), Arg674 (R674), Glu678 (E678), and Arg680 (R680) (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: Identified through structural modeling, contact analysis, and conservation analysis

claim: ZHX2 R581A and R674A mutants failed to rescue the cell growth defect in ZHX2 shRNA-infected MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Our cell proliferation data showed that consistent with our previous results, ZHX2 depletion led to decreased TNBC cell proliferation, and this phenotype was completely rescued by WT ZHX2. On the other hand, some of mutants (including R581A and R674A) failed to rescue the cell growth defect in ZHX2 shRNA-infected MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 6B

claim: ZHX2 R491A, R581A, and R674A mutants displayed a defect in cell growth in TNBC cell lines.
source: Motivated by our cell proliferation assay results, we further examined cell proliferation phenotypes using long-term 2D colony formation, 3D anchorage-independent growth, and cell invasion assays. ZHX2 R491A, R581A, and R674A mutants displayed a defect in cell growth in TNBC cell lines (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: Supported by 2D colony formation, 3D soft agar, and invasion assay data shown in Figure 6C–F

claim: Multiple residues (including R491, R581, and R674) may be important in regulating the phenotype of ZHX2 in TNBC.
source: In summary, our results showed that there may be multiple residues (including R491, R581, and R674) that may be important in regulating the phenotype of ZHX2 in TNBC.
evidence: Inferred from the functional assay results showing these mutants have defects

claim: Mutated ZHX2 (R581A and R674A) did not affect ZHX2 interaction with HIF1α.

evidence: Supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 6G

claim: ZHX2 mutants (R581A and R674A) led to increased HIF1α protein levels to the similar extent as wild type ZHX2.

evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6H

claim: ZHX2 mutations (R581A and R674A) led to decreased selective mRNA expression of HIF1α targeted genes.
source: In addition, these ZHX2 mutants led to increased HIF1α protein levels to the similar extent as wild type ZHX2 (Figure 6H), while qRT-PCR showed that the ZHX2 mutations indeed led to decreased selective mRNA expression of HIF1α targeted genes (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6I

claim: Residues R491, R581, and R674 are essential for mediating the transactivation of ZHX2 on HIF1α target genes.
